name: Romeo and Juliet
blurb: Shakespeare's tragedy of two young lovers from feuding families in Verona
aka: The Most Excellent and Lamentable Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
title: Romeo and Juliet Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: Romeo and Juliet summary: the feud, the secret marriage, Tybalt's death, Friar Laurence's plan and the tomb scene, act by act, with characters and themes.
h1: Romeo and Juliet: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, probably written between 1591 and 1595 and first printed in 1597. It is set in Verona, Italy, where the Montague and Capulet families have been enemies for generations. Romeo, a Montague, and Juliet, a Capulet, fall in love at first sight and marry in secret. The play follows how the feud, bad luck and haste turn their love into tragedy within a few days.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: The only son of the Montague family, a romantic young man
The only daughter of the Capulets, not yet fourteen
A Franciscan friar and Romeo's confidant, skilled with herbs and potions
Juliet's lifelong nurse and go-between, talkative and fond of her
Romeo's witty friend, a relative of the Prince
Romeo's cousin, who tries to keep the peace
Juliet's hot-tempered cousin, who hates the Montagues
A young count who wants to marry Juliet
The ruler of Verona, tired of the families' street fights

body: Act 1. A brawl between Montague and Capulet servants spreads through the streets of Verona, and Prince Escalus declares that anyone who disturbs the peace again will be put to death. Romeo is moping over Rosaline, who does not return his love. His cousin Benvolio and friend Mercutio persuade him to slip into a masked ball at the Capulet house, where Romeo sees Juliet and falls for her at once. They speak, kiss, and only afterwards learn that each belongs to the enemy family. Tybalt recognises Romeo at the party and wants to fight him, but Lord Capulet stops him.

Act 2. After the ball Romeo climbs into the Capulet orchard and hears Juliet on her balcony speaking of her love for him. They exchange vows and agree to marry. Friar Laurence agrees to marry them in secret, hoping the match will end the feud, and the Nurse carries messages between them. The next afternoon Romeo and Juliet are married in the friar's cell.

Act 3. That same day Tybalt challenges Romeo, who, now secretly his relative by marriage, refuses to fight. Mercutio takes up the challenge instead; when Romeo steps between them, Tybalt fatally wounds Mercutio under his arm. Mercutio dies cursing both houses, and Romeo in fury kills Tybalt. The Prince banishes Romeo from Verona. Romeo spends one night with Juliet before leaving for Mantua. Meanwhile Lord Capulet, believing Juliet's tears are for Tybalt, arranges for her to marry Paris in a few days and threatens to throw her out when she refuses. Even the Nurse advises her to forget Romeo.

Act 4. Juliet goes to Friar Laurence in despair. He gives her a potion that will make her appear dead for about forty-two hours. She will be laid in the family tomb, while he sends word to Romeo to come and take her away when she wakes. Juliet agrees to the wedding, drinks the potion that night, and is found apparently dead on the morning set for the marriage. The wedding turns into a funeral.

Act 5. Friar Laurence's letter never reaches Romeo: Friar John, who was to carry it, is shut in a house suspected of plague. Instead Romeo's servant Balthasar brings news that Juliet is dead. Romeo buys poison from a poor apothecary in Mantua and rides back to Verona. At the Capulet tomb he meets Paris, who has come to mourn, and kills him in a fight.

Inside the tomb Romeo kisses Juliet one last time, drinks the poison and dies. Friar Laurence arrives moments too late; Juliet wakes, sees Romeo dead, and refuses to leave with the friar, who flees at the sound of the watch. Finding no poison left, she stabs herself with Romeo's dagger. The Prince, the Capulets and Lord Montague gather at the tomb, where Montague reveals that his wife has died of grief over Romeo's exile. Friar Laurence explains everything, and Romeo's letter to his father confirms it. Montague and Capulet take each other's hands and promise golden statues of each other's child, and the Prince closes the play with the families finally at peace.

The Prologue calls the couple star-crossed and says their deaths will end the feud, so the audience knows the ending from the start. Readers debate whether the tragedy is caused by fate, with chance events such as the plague delay arriving at the worst moment, or by the characters' own choices: the hatred of the parents, Tybalt's temper and the lovers' speed, which Friar Laurence warns against. Another common reading treats the ending as a judgement on the older generation, whose feud costs them their children. Many readings combine these causes rather than choosing one.

ul: Love: the play shows love in several forms, from Romeo's crush on Rosaline to the Nurse's earthy jokes and the lovers' all-consuming devotion.
Hate and violence: the feud no one can explain drives the street fights, the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt, and finally the lovers' deaths.
Fate and chance: the star-crossed lovers seem doomed, and a delayed letter decides the ending.
Haste: the story covers only a few days, and the speed of every decision, from the marriage to the suicides, leaves no time for second thoughts.
Youth and age: the young lovers act on feeling, while parents and advisers fail them through anger, pressure or bad advice.
Length: five acts with a sonnet as prologue; it plays in about two and a half to three hours.

Sources and adaptations: Shakespeare adapted Arthur Brooke's poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562); famous retellings include Franco Zeffirelli's film (1968), Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet (1996) and the musical West Side Story.
Content: sword fights, several deaths and a double suicide.

What teachers usually ask about: who is to blame for the deaths, the role of fate, the balcony scene, Mercutio's cry of "A plague o' both your houses!", and how Friar Laurence and the Nurse fail Juliet.

check.q: Why does Romeo refuse to fight Tybalt at first?
options: The Prince has ordered him not to
He has just secretly married Juliet, Tybalt's cousin
check.why: Romeo now counts Tybalt as family, though no one else knows why.

check.q: Why does Romeo not learn of Friar Laurence's plan?
options: Friar John is kept in quarantine because of the plague
The Nurse forgets to deliver the letter
check.why: Friar John is shut in a house suspected of plague, so the letter never leaves Verona.

options: She drinks the rest of Romeo's poison
She stabs herself with Romeo's dagger
She takes a second sleeping potion
check.why: Romeo has left no poison in the vial, so she uses his dagger.

faq.q: How old are Romeo and Juliet?
faq.a: Juliet is thirteen; her Nurse and mother say she will turn fourteen in about two weeks. Romeo's age is never given, though he is described as a young man.

faq.q: How long does Romeo and Juliet take place over?
faq.a: The action covers only about four to five days, from the Sunday street fight to the deaths in the tomb later that week.

faq.q: Was Romeo and Juliet a true story?
faq.a: No. The story of two lovers from rival families in Verona was an Italian tale retold by several writers before Shakespeare, including Luigi da Porto and Matteo Bandello. Shakespeare's main source was Arthur Brooke's 1562 English poem.
